sources.claim: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity, so the owner can be held responsible for business debts; an LLC or corporation generally separates owners from business liability; the structure affects taxes and liability, and the SBA suggests talking with an attorney or accountant.

sections.skill: Recognize personal guarantees and how they bypass limited liability

questions.prompt: What is a personal guarantee?

choices.text: A promise to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot
A promise by the bank to lend you more money later
A guarantee that the business will make a profit this year
A warranty you give customers on a product

questions.correct_answer: A promise to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot
questions.intro: Limited liability has gaps. A PERSONAL GUARANTEE is a promise you sign to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot. Lenders, landlords and some suppliers often ask new business owners for one, because the business has little history. If you sign it, your personal savings and other assets can be used to pay that debt, even if you have an LLC. Personal guarantees can be hidden in long forms. Read before signing, ask what you are guaranteeing, and consider whether the amount is one you could pay personally.
questions.feedback: It makes you personally responsible for that debt.

questions.prompt: Co-signing means what?

choices.text: You can never be asked to pay anything at all
You may have to pay if the main borrower does not

questions.correct_answer: You may have to pay if the main borrower does not
questions.intro: Imagine co-signing a friend's phone contract. If your friend stops paying, the phone company can ask you to pay. A personal guarantee for your business works the same way: you are co-signing for your own company. Your LLC may be the main borrower, but your signature means you will pay if it cannot. That is why it matters so much.
questions.feedback: The co-signer backs the debt.
